items.title: SciMARS: Multi-Agent Recursive Self-Improvement for Closed-Loop Scientific Discovery
items.independence: Directly read saved official fulltext and official Atom identity metadata without adopting root/source-agent scope judgments.

summary_source_claims.quote: The optimizer seeks a harness that helps the team satisfy the task within B B . It observes public inputs, tool responses, candidate programs, and generated artifacts. It cannot query the official evaluator V V during revision. A host process calls V V after final commitment. A runnable program, completed tool call, or recorded finding does not establish task correctness. Public probes guide revision; official evaluation measures the final outcome.

The coordination component C t C_{t} contains routing flags and contracts for existing handoffs. A contract specifies a version, shared fields, a sender instruction, and a receiver instruction. A planner–coder contract can require observed array dimensions in the handoff. A role procedure can instead require the coder to check its inputs. The former changes handoffs; the latter changes role procedures.

A separate meta-level optimizer invokes the editors, composer, selector, and reflector. These are not executions of the seven-role team. The optimizer’s prompts, validators, selection algorithm, tools, and official evaluator remain outside the editable surface. The controller retains the current harness, task-local lessons L t L_{t} , and traces T t T_{t} . Accepted edits govern later rounds of the same task; they do not become a shared learned harness for later evaluation tasks.

Our shared memory draws on Mycelium’s active context-graph design ( Choudhury et al., 2026 ) . It lets a role retrieve evidence recorded by another role beyond the current handoff. We distinguish graph contents G t G_{t} from a memory policy M t M_{t} . The graph holds observations, interpretations, findings, hypotheses, plans, and unresolved questions. The policy determines what roles record and which records reach them. New findings change G t G_{t} ; retrieval rules belong to M t M_{t} .

The controller executes H t H_{t} to obtain reference evidence o t 0 o_{t}^{0} . Each editor receives the same current harness, task requirements, reference evidence, and retrieved lessons. No editor reads another editor’s proposal. SciMARS has two candidates:

The role editor changes role procedures while preserving coordination. The coordination editor changes at most one existing route or contract while preserving roles. Endpoint guidance belongs to the contract. An editor can retain the harness when evidence does not support change.

The memory editor receives a summary of the available graph and revises recording duties, retrieval filters, query hints, retrieval limits, or subscriptions. It preserves roles and coordination. The validator requires a version increase for changed policies and bounds retrieval limits between zero and twelve. These edits change access to evidence, not the evidence itself.

Probes use isolated workspaces or environment snapshots. Memory-enabled branches start from the same permitted seed and keep their writes separate. A public train–validation probe excludes held-out labels from the graph as well as from model inputs. Earlier live notes cannot enter such a probe if they encode those labels. Candidate probes provide evidence for comparison; stochastic executions do not establish a causal effect from one trial.

For interactive campaigns, the accepted harness governs subsequent live turns; probe artifacts do not replace the team’s acquired data. Composition and retention are distinct decisions. A proposed edit counts as retained only when selection adopts its harness.

Lessons guide the outer editors; the shared graph carries evidence among execution roles. Neither mechanism changes the optimizer itself. A new evaluation task resets adaptation state. A fixed development seed does not transfer evaluation-task updates.

Autonomous Science Bench reports separate GPT-6-Astra and GLM-5.3 cohorts. ScienceAgentBench and AppWorld use z-ai/glm-5.3-flashx , pinned to the Z.AI endpoint through OpenRouter with low reasoning effort and no provider fallback. Within each benchmark and model cohort, method–task runs share the same total model allowance, including execution, edits, probes, and selection.

The discovery evaluation uses experimental-data replay and a digital twin, not new physical wet-lab execution. Computational cost limits our evaluation to the tested language models, DS-STAR-based multi-agent configurations, and subsets of the benchmarks. Future work should evaluate additional base language models and multi-agent systems, as well as more complete benchmark suites, to assess the generality of the framework.

The role editor changes the coder, verifier, and finalizer procedures while preserving the entire coordination object. The coder must use the paths checked in the public trace. The verifier must check numerical output rather than file presence. The finalizer must preserve working code and recheck any rewrite. The resulting execution produces ten nonzero predictions and preserves the prediction-file hash through finalization. Its official mean absolute error (MAE) is 6.17 6.17 , compared with 78.0 78.0 for the round’s reference.

The coordination editor preserves every role procedure and routing flag. It adds one verifier.finalizer contract, which passes verification , code , and execution to the finalizer. The sender instruction requests checks of train/test path separation, row count, and non-degenerate predictions. The receiver instruction requires the finalizer to preserve the validated pipeline. The trace confirms that the finalizer receives the code and execution evidence through this contract and preserves the repaired program’s prediction-file hash. Its official MAE is 11.8 11.8 . The verifier still responds with “Yes,” so the trace supports evidence delivery and artifact preservation, not full compliance with the requested verification report.

summary_override.summary_en: SciMARS uses execution traces and public probes to revise team role procedures, handoff contracts, and, in its memory extension, evidence-recording and retrieval policies before composing and selecting a successor harness. Retained edits govern later improvement rounds of the same task; new evaluation tasks reset adaptation, so this is not cross-task accumulation. The optimizer itself stays fixed. summary_source_claims.quote: For a task x x , the Engineer uses evidence e e to sample a proposal trajectory τ E \tau_{\mathrm{E}} . Validation and fallback map it to the executed harness h = 𝒱 ⁡ ( τ E ) h=\mathcal{V}(\tau_{\mathrm{E}}) . The Solver acts under h h , producing trajectory τ S \tau_{\mathrm{S}} and terminal task reward R ⁡ ( x , τ S ) R(x,\tau_{\mathrm{S}}) . For role i ∈ { E , S } i\in\{\mathrm{E},\mathrm{S}\} , θ i \theta_{i} and ϕ i \phi_{i} are actor and critic parameters, with actor policy π θ i \pi_{\theta_{i}} . Indices t t , b b , and k k denote generated-token positions, paired episodes, and saved checkpoints, respectively; θ S ( k ) \theta_{\mathrm{S}}^{(k)} and h k h_{k} identify saved weights and code. The no-harness condition ∅ \varnothing retains the base executor.

For a task x x , the Engineer receives historical feedback e e and samples a proposal trajectory τ E \tau_{\mathrm{E}} . Validation and fallback map that proposal to the executed harness h = 𝒱 ⁡ ( τ E ) h=\mathcal{V}(\tau_{\mathrm{E}}) . The Solver then interacts with the environment under h h , producing trajectory τ S \tau_{\mathrm{S}} and task reward R ⁡ ( x , τ S ) R(x,\tau_{\mathrm{S}}) . An invalid proposal maps to h = ∅ h=\varnothing , retaining the base executor.

The same reward trains both policies: the Engineer learns which harnesses support successful execution, while the Solver learns how to complete tasks under those harnesses. Each policy is updated on its own generated outputs, without differentiating through harness execution. We use a KL-regularized SAO-based actor–critic backbone ( Hou et al., 2026 ) , with a fixed reference policy for each role. The local realization retains behavior–proximal token-ratio decoupling.

The Engineer generates a harness once, whereas the Solver acts over multiple turns. Their different output lengths and KL penalties can produce different return scales despite the shared task reward. Writing the raw, unweighted critic target as G i , t G_{i,t} , we normalize critic targets separately for each role:

Solver-only rounds freeze the Engineer’s parameters but still sample fresh harnesses. They use unit partner weights. Thus, the Solver continues learning under sampled harnesses while their generating policy remains fixed.
Algorithm 1 summarizes the procedure. At deployment, we select a saved harness and evaluate it with a frozen Solver checkpoint.

Algorithm 1 Joint learning of the Engineer and Solver 0: Engineer and Solver policies, independent critics, reference policies, task/evidence stream 1: for each training round do 2: Choose active roles according to Schedule. 3: Engineer samples a code proposal from historical feedback. 4: Validate it to obtain the executed harness and run the Solver. 5: Record both outputs and their shared task reward. 6: for each active role do 7: Estimate values using Context and ValueNorm. 8: Compute and standardize advantages. 9: Apply Peer weights and update the actor through the SAO-based path. 10: Update the critic on normalized return targets. 11: end for 12: end for 13: Select a saved harness and Solver checkpoint for evaluation.

Except for locally evaluated JoMoHa and WHALE, scores are taken from Harness-R1 ( Shao et al., 2026 ) ; we use its training and test sets, with checkpoint and harness selection on a separate validation set. The task model is Qwen3.5-9B; frontier model names denote harness editors, not replacement Solvers. Agent SFT + Harness-R1 additionally fine-tunes the task model, while WHALE uses its RSFT-plus-search recipe. WHALE alternates after eight environment interactions (16 training steps), uses the same harness-search settings as JoMoHa , and matches its total environment-interaction budget. Section 6.2 examines one-sided learning, frozen-Engineer training, program swaps, and coordination components.

Learning curves alone cannot separate improvements in Solver ability from improvements in the generated runtime. We therefore cross-evaluate saved programs and Solver checkpoints (Table 5 ). At the later Solver, replacing the initial program with the later program raises success from 92.5% to 96.5%, without changing model weights. Relative to no harness, the later program gains 5.0 points, with no observed success-to-failure regressions on this evaluation set. The earlier and later learned programs also both improve the earlier Solver from 91.5% under the initial program to 95.0%. These results show that the saved programs contribute useful behavior beyond the initial runtime, including at a different Solver checkpoint. The equal 95.0% scores on the earlier Solver, but 95.0% versus 96.5% on the later Solver, further show that program value depends on the Solver with which it is paired.

Table 5: Harness utility at fixed Solver weights. Fixed-program cross-evaluation: columns fix Solvers and rows fix programs. Earlier and later denote programs and Solvers saved at checkpoints 48 and 144, respectively. The initial program comes from the initial Engineer. Colors follow Table 4 . Harness Earlier Solver Later Solver No harness 90.0 91.5 Initial program 91.5 92.5 Earlier program 95.0 95.0 Later program 95.0 96.5

summary_override.summary_en: JoMoHa trains an Engineer that generates executable harnesses and a task-solving Solver using task outcomes. Historical feedback conditions code proposals, which are validated before execution. Saved programs and model checkpoints are selected on validation and frozen for evaluation; program swaps at fixed Solver weights examine the contribution of the code. Its coevolution evidence includes retained and reused code artifacts beyond model learning, without establishing continual self-modification at deployment or local reruns of every cited baseline.

items.title: MIRIX-2.0: Multi-Agent Memory System
items.independence: Directly read official fulltext and metadata, tested the requested scope boundaries against quoted counterevidence, and authored conservative bilingual summaries. Root supplied candidate names and proposed narrow branches, not adopted as evidence.
items.review_scope: Official identity/date/abstract matching; direct reading of method, protocol and limitation passages; scope adjudication and qualitative summary verification. No experimental rerun or whole-paper numerical recalculation.

summary_source_claims.quote: where Δ u \Delta_{u} is the newly written semantic frontier and G ~ u \widetilde{G}_{u} is the consolidated hypergraph. The evidence store P u P_{u} is returned unchanged. On procedural memory it starts in the background once five task sessions are pending, and it turns them into skills.

Semantic Dream never rewrites the memories in the vector database, and it consolidates neither episodic-only anchors nor fact nodes. The asymmetry is deliberate. Semantic identity can be refined incrementally, whereas event occurrences and their citations are kept as observations. AutoDream therefore makes the graph less fragmented without creating a textual summary whose embedding could hide the details of its inputs.

For procedural memory, AutoDream refines instead of merging. A distiller judges the outcome of each pending session from quotes in its transcript and distills experiences e 1 , … , e m e_{1},\ldots,e_{m} , each marked as a lesson worth reusing or a mistake worth avoiding. A curator ( Zhang et al., 2026c ) turns these experiences into skills in the procedural store P u P P_{u}^{P} , and it can create, edit, or delete a skill. An edit can cite the experiences behind it with a quote of the text it adds, and a citation is recorded only when that quote checks out, so a cited step of a skill can be traced through its experiences to the quoted sessions they came from. In Figure 3 , one failed purchase yields an experience to avoid and one to reuse, and the curator adds two steps to the shopping routine that cite the first and keeps a step that the second supports. The distiller’s unclear verdict and the curator’s non-edit verdicts are in Section A.5 . \FloatBarrier

The conversational tables report all three configurations. The available document QA results and graph efficiency measurements use M1 and are labeled accordingly; disabling AutoDream there is an experimental choice, not a restriction that prevents consolidation of document memories. MemoryCD is reported under the system name, but its recorded results do not identify an M0, M1, or M2 configuration, so we do not use them to estimate the contribution of AutoDream. For agent memory, we evaluate the procedural refinement path, in which AutoDream distills sessions into reusable skills whose retrieval is independent of the semantic hypergraph. The M0, M1, and M2 comparisons below therefore concern user-memory indexing and semantic consolidation, rather than a procedural graph ablation.

We evaluate procedural memory on ALFWorld ( Shridhar et al., 2021 ) and WebShop ( Yao et al., 2022 ) , comparing an agent without memory with ReasoningBank ( Ouyang et al., 2026 ) , Agent Workflow Memory (AWM) ( Wang et al., 2025e ) , and MIRIX-2.0 . Within each comparison, methods share the actor prompt and backbone. ALFWorld uses GPT-6 Luna and GPT-5.6 Luna; WebShop uses GPT-6 Luna. Each memory method learns from the same training tasks, 39 for ALFWorld and 40 for WebShop. Memory is then frozen for evaluation on 134 held-out ALFWorld episodes with a 50-step cap and 140 WebShop instructions with a 15-step cap. Results are averaged over three independent runs. The separation between memory learning and evaluation tests reuse of acquired procedures on new tasks.

This setting exercises the procedural branch of AutoDream (Section 2.5 ). Sessions supply lessons to reuse and mistakes to avoid, and a curator turns those experiences into skills. Unlike semantic consolidation, which preserves the factual records and changes their index, procedural refinement changes the instructions available to the actor. The experiments evaluate the utility of that combined process; they do not separately ablate the outcome judge, experience distiller, or curator.

The step counts provide a complementary view. Successful episodes require 13.2 rather than 14.2 steps with GPT-6 Luna and 12.4 rather than 16.1 with GPT-5.6 Luna, relative to no memory. This is consistent with more direct action sequences, but the successful subsets differ across methods, so these are not paired measurements on identical solved tasks. The large success-rate standard deviations for MIRIX-2.0 , 6.2 and 14.0 points, also limit the conclusion. It has the highest observed mean, but three runs do not establish a stable advantage over AWM.

Table 3 evaluates agent memory on Part I of MetaClaw-Bench ( Xia et al., 2026b ) , which spans 30 days. Accuracy is the official mean per-question score, which combines binary file checks with partial credit on multiple-choice questions, and completion is the completion rate over the 224 file-check questions. With GPT-5.2, MIRIX-2.0 improves the official mean question score from 44.0% for MetaClaw Skills to 49.2%, and file-check completion from 17.1% to 27.7%. The larger completion gain, 10.6 points, suggests that reusable procedures can help produce the required artifacts as well as improve question scores. With Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, the score gain is smaller, from 51.8% to 52.7%, and completion is tied at 30.8%. The benefit therefore depends on the backbone and on what the metric measures. The GPT-5.2 baselines are reported values from the MetaClaw paper, so this comparison is not evidence from a fully controlled rerun. Unlike ALFWorld and WebShop, this table does not report variation across independent runs or a matched procedural-component ablation.

Two rules of the procedural path complete Section 2.5 . The distiller judges the outcome of each pending session from quotes in its transcript, and an outcome whose quotes do not occur in the transcript is downgraded to unclear rather than trusted. Besides creating, editing, or deleting a skill, the curator can mark an experience as already covered, not worth a skill, or deferred, so it can decline an experience without changing the store. The quote check on outcomes and the quote check on citations are the procedural counterpart of the provenance that the hypergraph keeps for facts. They keep the skill library traceable although both Distill ⋆ \textsc{Distill}^{\star} and Curate ⋆ \textsc{Curate}^{\star} in Algorithm 1 are language-model calls.

The tables evaluate complete configurations, so the component explanations in this section remain interpretations, and the limitations in Section 5 list the ablations that would test them. The tables also do not measure merge precision, source-detail retention, skill provenance coverage, or the contribution of the six-writer routing policy, and they do not report memory length or user-memory ingestion tokens, for which graph counts and answer tokens cannot substitute.

summary_override.summary_zh: MIRIX 的 AutoDream 程序性技能分支根据会话轨迹判断成败，再由 curator 创建、编辑或删除供后续 Agent 使用的技能指令。训练任务形成的技能库冻结后，在新任务上评估复用。纳入依据是反馈驱动的程序性步骤修订，语义记录合并与事实检索不属于这条证据；实验评估的是整套流程，未单独证明每次技能修改或某个组件的收益。
summary_override.summary_en: The procedural-skill branch of MIRIX AutoDream judges session outcomes from execution transcripts, then uses a curator to create, edit, or delete skill instructions for later agents. Skills acquired on training tasks are frozen and evaluated for reuse on new tasks. Inclusion rests on feedback-driven revision of procedural steps, separate from semantic-record consolidation and factual retrieval. The experiments evaluate the combined process, without isolating the benefit of every skill edit or individual component.

items.title: When Experience Becomes a Backdoor: Poisoning Self-Evolving LLM Agents via Failure-Aware Task Optimization

summary_source_claims.quote: A self-evolving agent consists of a solver 𝒜 sol \mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{sol}} that executes tasks and an evolver 𝒜 evo \mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{evo}} that updates the agent’s harness (e.g., prompts, skills, or memory) from execution experience. We focus on skill-based self-evolution [ 24 , 30 , 38 , 16 ] , where the evolver updates persistent skills while other harness components remain fixed.

Formally, let S S denote a skill state, i.e., the set of skills available to the solver. Given a task x x , the solver executes it with S S and produces an execution experience e x = ( τ x , o x ) = 𝒜 sol ​ ( x , S ) e_{x}=(\tau_{x},o_{x})=\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{sol}}(x,S) , where τ x \tau_{x} and o x o_{x} denote the execution trajectory and the task outcome, respectively. Let 𝒟 evolve \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{evolve}} and 𝒟 test \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{test}} denote the evolution and test task sets, respectively. Starting from an initial skill state S 0 S_{0} , the agent evolves its skills on 𝒟 evolve \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{evolve}} batch by batch: for each batch 𝒟 t ⊆ 𝒟 evolve \mathcal{D}_{t}\subseteq\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{evolve}} , the solver executes its tasks with the current skills, and the evolver updates the skills from the resulting experience:

After all T T batches, the evolved skill state is denoted as S T = Evolve ⁡ ( S 0 , 𝒟 evolve ) S_{T}=\operatorname{Evolve}(S_{0},\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{evolve}}) , which the solver then uses on 𝒟 test \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{test}} .

We assume the attacker knows the self-evolution mechanism and has access to 𝒟 evolve \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{evolve}} and a validation set 𝒟 val \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{val}} , disjoint from 𝒟 evolve \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{evolve}} and 𝒟 test \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{test}} , for evaluating candidate poisoned tasks. The attacker has no access to 𝒟 test \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{test}} , the victim’s backbone LLMs, its evolved skills, or the trajectories of its solver and evolver. Given a poisoning budget B B , the attacker can only inject up to B B poisoned tasks 𝒟 poison \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{poison}} into 𝒟 evolve \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{evolve}} , yielding the poisoned evolution task set:

Datasets. We conduct experiments on three public benchmarks widely used by recent skill-based self-evolution frameworks [ 30 , 24 , 38 ] : SpreadsheetBench (SB) [ 23 ] for real-world spreadsheet manipulation, and WikiTQ [ 26 ] and OfficeQA [ 25 ] for question answering over tables and documents. Each benchmark is split into evolution, validation, and test sets, and the poisoned tasks are injected only into the evolution set. The statistics and more details of the datasets are given in Appendix 10.1 .

Self-Evolution Frameworks and LLM Backbones. We evaluate BadEvolve on four skill-based self-evolution frameworks, i.e., Trace2Skill [ 24 ] , SkillGrad [ 38 ] , SkillOpt [ 30 ] , and A-Evolve [ 18 ] . We consider four backbones of different families and scales, i.e., Kimi-K2.5 [ 12 ] , GPT-OSS-120B [ 1 ] , Claude Sonnet 4.6 [ 2 ] , and Qwen3-235B [ 45 ] . More details are given in Appendix 10.3 .

Evaluation Protocol. We consider the two attack objectives in Sec. 3.2 , i.e., Payload Injection (PI) and Answer Corruption (AC). For each attack, the victim agent evolves from S 0 S_{0} on 𝒟 evolve p \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{evolve}}^{p} in three independent runs. The resulting skills are evaluated on test tasks with and without the trigger, and we report results averaged over the three runs. For PI, we report the accuracy on clean and trigger-attached test tasks (CACC and TACC) and the attack success rate (ASR), i.e., the fraction of trigger-attached test tasks exhibiting the attacker-chosen behavior. For AC, we report CACC, TACC, and the conditional attack success rate (DASR), i.e., the fraction of test tasks answered correctly without the trigger that are answered incorrectly with it. To assess utility, we also report CACC 0 , the test accuracy of skills evolved on 𝒟 evolve \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{evolve}} only. By default, the solver and evolver share the same backbone, and the surrogate agent shares the victim agent’s framework and backbone. More details are in Appendix 10.4 .

We consider four skill-based self-evolution frameworks. Specifically, Trace2Skill [ 24 ] consolidates lessons from successful and failed trajectories into a skill directory provided to the solver by default. SkillGrad [ 38 ] diagnoses errors in a batch of trajectories and patches a single skill in place, accepting every patch. SkillOpt [ 30 ] also patches the skill in place, but accepts a patch only if it does not decrease the score on a held-out set, for which we use the validation split. A-Evolve [ 18 ] maintains multiple skills that the evolver can create, refine, or merge, and the solver loads skills on demand from a catalog, so an induced rule takes effect only if its skill is loaded.

During optimization, each candidate poisoned instruction is evaluated with K = 5 K=5 independent self-evolution runs of the surrogate agent from S 0 S_{0} . After each run, the solver executes every validation task both with and without the trigger. J ^ obj \widehat{J}_{\mathrm{obj}} averages the attack success over runs and validation tasks: for PI, success is counted whenever the payload appears, regardless of answer correctness; for AC, J ^ obj = 1 − TACC \widehat{J}_{\mathrm{obj}}=1-\mathrm{TACC} . Likewise, the stage-wise pass rates 𝐩 ^ \hat{\mathbf{p}} in Eq. ( 8 ) are averaged over the K K runs. The final results are reported on the test tasks, each evaluated with and without the trigger, following the protocol in Sec. 5.1 ; the sizes of all splits are given in Tab. 6 .

In this paper, we study a novel problem of task-level backdoor attacks against self-evolving LLM agents, where the attacker can only inject poisoned evolution tasks to induce the agent to implant backdoors into its own skills. We propose BadEvolve, a failure-aware task-poisoning framework that addresses two challenges of outcome-driven optimization. Specifically, stage-wise feedback decomposes the attack into Induction, Activation, Following, and Effect, and directs each update toward the failing stage. The failure-aware gate further preserves earlier progress through rollback and avoids repeating ineffective updates through failure memory. Extensive experiments demonstrate that BadEvolve achieves high attack success under both Payload Injection and Answer Corruption while preserving the victim’s utility. In the future, we will extend BadEvolve to other harness components such as memories and prompts, and study defenses against such task-level backdoor attacks.

summary_override.summary_zh: BadEvolve 检验技能自演化系统是否会把受污染的演化任务转成持续影响后续行为的规则，威胁模型不允许攻击者直接修改受害者技能。被测演化器从执行轨迹与任务结果更新技能，并在后续测试任务中复用；实验分别评估普通任务和带触发条件的任务。它属于 Harness 专项安全评测，结论限于所测技能演化框架与威胁模型，不能推广为所有提示或记忆组件都已验证存在同样问题。
summary_override.summary_en: BadEvolve examines whether skill-evolving agents can turn poisoned evolution tasks into rules that persist into later behavior, under a threat model that prevents direct modification of victim skills. The evaluated evolvers update skills from execution traces and outcomes, then reuse them on test tasks; clean and trigger-attached tasks are assessed separately. This is Harness-specific security evaluation whose findings are limited to the tested skill-evolution frameworks and threat model, rather than every prompt or memory component.

items.title: Trustworthy Recursive Self-Improvement with Statistical Guarantees
items.independence: Directly read official fulltext and metadata, tested the requested scope boundaries against quoted counterevidence, and authored conservative bilingual summaries. Root supplied candidate names and proposed narrow branches, not adopted as evidence.

summary_source_claims.quote: We consider a self-improvement process that starts with an initial incumbent solver Θ 0 \Theta_{0} and initial information ℱ 0 \mathcal{F}_{0} . It recursively generates and evaluates candidates over T T rounds. In round t t , let Q ( ⋅ ∣ ℱ t − 1 ) Q(\cdot\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}) denote the conditional distribution of the candidate given the completed history ℱ t − 1 \mathcal{F}_{t-1} from the fixed proposer. The proposer generates Θ ~ t ∼ Q ( ⋅ ∣ ℱ t − 1 ) \widetilde{\Theta}_{t}\sim Q\!\left(\cdot\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}\right) , which is evaluated by the gate 𝒢 \mathcal{G} against the previous incumbent Θ t − 1 \Theta_{t-1} . Then the gate 𝒢 \mathcal{G} produces A t ∈ { 0 , 1 } A_{t}\in\{0,1\} and updates the incumbent according to

Different gates may induce different acceptance decisions, thereby changing the subsequent self-improvement trajectories and the candidates proposed in later rounds. These changes can affect the final gain, which is defined as

Here, FER is the expected proportion of unacceptably inferior updates among accepted updates, and ε \varepsilon specifies the tolerated loss. For ε > 0 \varepsilon>0 , the difference Δ t \Delta_{t} is divided into three regions: updates with Δ t ≤ − ε \Delta_{t}\leq-\varepsilon are unacceptable, those with − ε < Δ t ≤ 0 -\varepsilon<\Delta_{t}\leq 0 are tolerated but not improving, and those with Δ t > 0 \Delta_{t}>0 are improving. Our goal is to ensure that FER ε ⁡ ( T ) ≤ q \operatorname{FER}_{\varepsilon}(T)\leq q for a prespecified FER budget q q , thereby providing a statistical safety guarantee for the entire self-improvement process. This helps avoid unacceptable updates, retain beneficial proposals, and may achieve a favorable final gain.
If the null hypothesis H t 0 H_{t}^{0} is rejected, the selected candidate is accepted as the new incumbent. Otherwise, the previous incumbent is retained.

In online FDR control, testing levels are allocated across multiple hypotheses under an overall error budget ( Chen and Kasiviswanathan, 2020 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ) . TRUST adapts this framework to the sequence of candidate acceptance tests defined in ( 5 ), using q q as the total FER budget. In round t t , the testing level α t \alpha_{t} determines the acceptance threshold, while the test statistic M t , m ( β ) M_{t,m}^{(\beta)} measures the evidence accumulated from the first m m validation observations. For α t > 0 \alpha_{t}>0 , TRUST accepts the candidate at the first m ≤ n m\leq n when M t , m ( β ) ≥ 1 / α t M_{t,m}^{(\beta)}\geq 1/\alpha_{t} , following the standard testing rule for sequential e-value testing ( Ramdas et al., 2023 ) . If the threshold is not reached within n n observations, the incumbent is retained. When α t = 0 \alpha_{t}=0 , validation is skipped and the incumbent is retained. We next describe how α t \alpha_{t} is allocated and how M t , m ( β ) M_{t,m}^{(\beta)} is constructed.

We next describe how to determine ρ t \rho_{t} . Building on the contextual error budget allocation in online multiple hypothesis testing ( Chen and Kasiviswanathan, 2020 ) , we make use of the context C t C_{t} in round t t and use an LLM to analyze it. This context only contains information available before the current round’s validation, including the candidate update and feedback from previous validation rounds. Following the evaluation structure of G-Eval ( Liu et al., 2023 ) , the LLM uses explicit criteria to assess the candidate’s potential benefits and risks. Let Ψ \Psi denote the mapping from context to LLM multipliers, with w t = Ψ ⁡ ( C t ) ∈ [ 0 , ∞ ) w_{t}=\Psi(C_{t})\in[0,\infty) . The default spending fraction is set to ρ t 0 = 1 / ( T − t + 1 ) \rho_{t}^{0}=1/(T-t+1) , corresponding to an equal share of the remaining FER budget. The LLM multiplier adjusts the spending fraction within the range [ ρ min , ρ max ] [\rho_{\min},\rho_{\max}] :

Reusing validation feedback to construct or select later candidates can lead to optimistic bias in their estimated performance, which is widely studied in adaptive data analysis ( Dwork et al., 2015 ; Rogers et al., 2016 ) . We use β \beta to represent the strength of the correction for data reuse. Assumption 1 connects this correction to our testing by bounding the conditional mean in the e-value construction. We discuss the relationship between β \beta and our algorithm in detail in Appendix A.1 .

Theorem 2 controls the expected proportion of unacceptable updates among all accepted updates over the entire self-improvement process with T T rounds. The same bound in ( 13 ) holds with T T replaced by any stopping time τ ≤ T \tau\leq T with respect to the self-improvement history ( ℱ t ) t = 0 T (\mathcal{F}_{t})_{t=0}^{T} , as established in Appendix C.2 . Thus, the process may be stopped based on the observed self-improvement history without losing FER control. In addition, the FER guarantee does not rely on the LLM correctly identifying beneficial candidates. The LLM uses context to allocate more FER budget to promising candidates and less to unpromising ones, safely improving the detection of beneficial updates.

The present study does not address how to identify an exact value of overlap correction strength from data or how to optimally tune other parameters. The noninferiority margin provides an interpretable tolerance for loss, but the theoretical guarantee can be conservative and only partly explains practical behavior. The LLM allocator can occasionally make mistakes when judging candidate updates, which may lead to poor choices of LLM multipliers. Optimizing the gate to maximize gain while keeping safety metrics within target ranges is also a promising direction. Future work can address these limitations to make the recursive self-improvement process more trustworthy and effective.

Motivated by prior work on modular reasoning, decomposition, self-refinement, and prompt scope ( Zhou et al., 2023 ; Madaan et al., 2023 ; Fernando et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2024 ) , we represent the reasoning strategy as an explicit and editable rule set. The corresponding operators allow reasoning rules and decomposition policies to be added, revised, generalized, reprioritized, or removed based on closed historical feedback. The particular typed rule schema and operator definitions are implementation choices of our harness.

Motivated by retrieval-augmented generation, adaptive retrieval, evolving retrieval policies, and selective context construction ( Lewis et al., 2020 ; Asai et al., 2024 ; Huang et al., 2026 ; Ye et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2023 ) , we treat routing as an editable pre-solver information-access policy. Its operators control how available context is selected, ranked, expanded, truncated, or restored before the solver call.

Drawing on automated and evolutionary workflow optimization ( Zhang et al., 2025a ; Zhao et al., 2026 ) , we treat the within-call execution workflow as an editable state that can evolve across rounds through changes to verification, evidence alignment, stopping, and fallback policies.

We evaluate Greedy, PACE, SGM-B, SGM-H, and TRUST on HotpotQA, DROP, and APPS with Qwen-3.8-Flash and DeepSeek-V4-Flash. Each method runs for 30 outer rounds. For HotpotQA, DROP, and APPS, solver output seeds range from 0 to 4 and data split seeds range from 42 to 46. Within each setting, all methods share the same initial test responses. Throughout the experiments, we reuse cached responses for identical inputs whenever possible to ensure fair comparisons across methods. One candidate is then selected for validation on up to 40 examples sampled without replacement from the 200-example validation pool; validation samples may overlap across rounds. The initial set contains 20 examples and the validation pool contains 200 examples. All four components and 20 operators in Appendix F are available. Performance is evaluated on 300 held-out test examples, which are used only for reporting.

In each setting, all gates start from the same initial harness, which contains prespecified weaknesses that provide clear opportunities for improvement. This design allows us to examine whether different gates accept candidates that correct these weaknesses. In later rounds, when the incumbent has typically reached a higher level of performance, we also examine whether the gates reject subsequent candidates that could reduce performance and cause the agent to lose earlier gains. The experiments therefore examine different stages of the RSI process, from repairing initial weaknesses to preserving improvements during continued search.

The proposer generates three proposals using feedback from completed rounds. We screen the candidates on 20 examples from the previous round and select the valid candidate with the highest score for the current round. To minimize the effect of unequal feedback sample sizes on the proposer, we retain all 40 examples for feedback even when TRUST’s statistical test stops early. Exposure probabilities in subsequent rounds therefore account for the full batch rather than only the observations up to the stopping time.

summary_override.summary_en: TRUST organizes admission of Harness candidates as statistical tests across rounds. Historical feedback guides rule or policy revisions, and paired validation outcomes must accumulate sufficient evidence before replacing the incumbent. An LLM allocates testing budget from information available before validation, while test data are used only for reporting. Its guarantees depend on assumptions about bias from reused validation samples and a tolerated loss margin; they control an expected proportion of unacceptable acceptances, not improvement after every accepted update.

items.title: How Much Skill Orchestration Can LLM Agents Compile Away? Execution-Grounded Specialization for Token-Efficient Skill Use
items.independence: Directly read official fulltext and metadata, tested the requested scope boundaries against quoted counterevidence, and authored conservative bilingual summaries. Root supplied candidate names and proposed narrow branches, not adopted as evidence.
items.review_scope: Official identity/date/abstract matching; direct reading of method, protocol and limitation passages; scope adjudication and qualitative summary verification. No experimental rerun or whole-paper numerical recalculation.

summary_source_claims.quote: SkillCache performs branch-level specialization of a supplied skill using one completed invocation. It works in three phases. (1) Observe : It records the cold invocation’s observable trace τ obs \tau_{\mathrm{obs}} , which holds the tool calls with their arguments, results, and errors, and the agent’s messages. The trace identifies the branch the skill took and carries its runtime arguments, intermediate observations, and recovery actions. (2) Compile : An isolated compiler turns τ obs \tau_{\mathrm{obs}} into a capsule , fusing adjacent deterministic tool calls into programs, keeping judgments as natural-language steps, and lifting request-dependent values into bindings (Figure 2 ). The host admits a capsule only after its programs pass a replay in the task’s sandbox, and otherwise falls back to a written procedure (Section 5 ). (3) Execute : In a later, warm execution, a plan executor runs the programs and hands natural-language steps and failed programs to the model (Section 6 ). Each phase runs in a fresh sandbox, and no phase sees the benchmark’s tests or verifier (Appendix A.3 ).

These phases follow a tracing JIT compiler (Section 2.2 ). The cold execution is the recorded path, and the capsule is the compiled trace, kept for later requests of the same kind as a trace cache keeps compiled traces ( Gal et al., 2009 ) . SkillCache’s compiler is an LLM agent that can write failing programs, which is why the host replays each candidate before admitting it. A program can still fail later when the request, the model’s decisions, or the environment differ. Like a failed guard, a failed program leaves the compiled path through deoptimization, but only for that step, and the rest of the plan stays compiled.

Each binding describes how to obtain its live value, from the request or workspace, a natural-language step, or a program’s output. Each program declares the bindings it reads and those it sets for later programs, so values pass from one program to the next without the model. Programs are language-agnostic. Each has source files, a command, and a syntax or build check, reads its inputs from a JSON file, and prints one JSON result or exits nonzero with a diagnostic.

The compiler reads ( q , S , τ obs ) (q,S,\tau_{\mathrm{obs}}) in a fresh sandbox that holds none of the task’s files. The compiler prompt and the program interface are fixed across tasks, and the prompt (Appendix B ) specifies four specialization rules. Path pruning : The compiler removes failed exploration, keeps the skill’s requirements, and adds no behavior that neither the skill nor the trace shows. Binding lifting : Values that a program needs and that depend on the request or workspace become bindings, each with an instruction for obtaining its live value, while other values stay as the execution used them. Region fusion : Deterministic operations become programs, and adjacent ones share one program. Where the execution ran code, such as a skill’s script, the program reuses that code and changes only the bindings. A step that needs semantic judgment or a new observation stays a natural-language step. Grounded postconditions : V V checks only the observable postconditions that the request and source skill state, together with any inspection by which the execution checked and corrected its own result. The prompt forbids comparing a result with the answer the observed execution produced, and the compiler never sees the evaluator.

Gate 3: End-to-end replay. In a fresh task sandbox, the host replays the plan with the same plan executor used at reuse. The examples E E supply every binding that no program outputs. Programs execute on task inputs and pass their outputs through the bindings. If a program fails, replay records its diagnostics, substitutes its observed outputs from E E , and continues to collect failures from later programs in the same replay.

The compiler receives the collected failures and its previous answer, then returns a repaired capsule. The host allows up to three attempts at the hybrid form, a capsule with programs. If no candidate qualifies, the host compiles the same trace into a written procedure, the textual form, with a prompt that follows the same rules. If that also fails, later executions run with the source skill alone. Appendix B gives the prompts for both forms.

If the model called each program itself, it would still read the whole plan from the start and orchestrate every call. A capsule, however, explicitly interleaves program steps with natural-language steps and declares each program’s input and output bindings. This structure lets consecutive programs run back to back without invoking the model. We thus introduce an executor-driven design, in which a plan executor, skillcache-run , advances through the program steps and returns control to the model when the plan needs its input or judgment. The executor runs each program through the runtime, skillcache-tool . Both skillcache-run and skillcache-tool are command-line programs that the host places in the agent’s sandbox, and the model invokes them with its ordinary shell tool, so the agent harness runs unchanged. In the alternative agent-driven backend, the prompt holds the whole plan and the model calls skillcache-tool for each program itself (Figure 4 ).

A compiled program can fail on a later request, for example when a service is down or an input differs from the observed one. A program fails when it exits nonzero twice, runs out of time, or returns without an output it declares. The executor then hands that step to the model as program_failed , with its instruction and diagnostics. For a step of π \pi (Equation 4 ), it also gives the path of the program’s source, which shows how the step was done. Only the failing step leaves the compiled path, and the rest of the plan continues compiled. The model then performs that step itself, with the source skills still available as in a cold execution. In the main runs, the executor hands back a failed program in 11 of 481 warm executions of hybrid capsules (Appendix A.5 ).

Metrics. We report provider-reported tokens, which include cache reads and writes, list-price cost, model calls, latency, and verifier reward. Reward is the task verifier’s score in [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] , which is 1 when every check passes, and a few tasks give partial credit. Latency is the span from a task’s first model call to the end of its last, so it includes the commands and programs between calls. A missing outcome scores zero reward, and tokens, cost, and calls cover the tasks on which every context (cold included) recorded tokens and reward. Warm executions exclude the compile cost because a one-trace capsule is compiled after its request is served. We report this cost separately and amortize it over reuses in Section 7.6 . Because a few long tasks can dominate totals, we also count the tasks on which one context is better or worse, taking each task’s three-run mean.

Setup. Because SkillsBench gives each task a single request, we additionally build three kinds of probes, each changing one thing in a source task, to test whether a capsule still works when a recurring request changes. An instance probe changes the input content or a parameter the request states, a rename probe changes the paths of files the request names, and a reword probe rewrites one to three sentences of the request. A probe is kept only if, in its task’s container, its reference solution passes its verifier and, for an instance probe, the source task’s reference answer fails. We build 23 instance, 19 rename, and 24 reword probes for 24 of the 44 tasks whose cold execution succeeded in the first Sonnet run, all of which also succeeded with Opus (Appendix A.9 ). We start from successful cold executions to test whether the resulting capsules can carry a successful execution path over to a changed request.

Results. Capsules stay effective when the request changes and keep their token savings (Table 4 ). Averaged over three runs, tokens decrease by 70 to 87% for every probe type with both models, and mean reward changes by +0.01 to +0.15. On instance probes, where the original answer would fail, tokens decrease by 82% with Sonnet and 72% with Opus while reward stays comparable. With DeepSeek-V4-Flash running the same Opus capsules, tokens decrease by 71% and mean reward rises from 0.54 to 0.92 across all probes (Appendix A.9 ). One failure case comes from three Sonnet capsules that hard-code request-dependent values, causing wrong answers on the corresponding instance probes. This highlights the need for generated programs to use request-dependent values through bindings.

In our study, all experiments use SkillsBench and the Claude Code harness. We see broader potential in the idea of compiling a completed execution into programs that an executor drives on later requests. It could also benefit recurring agent tasks without skills or in other harnesses. Extending SkillCache to these settings is one direction for future work.

SkillCache also incurs a one-time compilation cost and is most useful when later requests amortize it (Section 7.6 ). In addition, each capsule is compiled from one cold execution and may carry useful patterns alongside brittle assumptions, errors, or biases. Replay in qualification also runs the programs only with the original request’s values and inputs, so a capsule that hard-codes one of those values can still pass, as the instance probes in Section 7.5 show. Future work could let a capsule learn from its warm executions and improve with use, much as a tracing JIT compiles paths it discovers later ( Gal et al., 2009 ) .

Finally, as SkillsBench supplies each task’s skills, our evaluation supplies each task’s capsule and does not test retrieval. Production use would require reliable retrieval and selection as the cache grows, along with execution safeguards and cache invalidation when a skill or its environment changes. Integrating these lifecycle and security mechanisms in persistent deployments is another direction for future work.

Every phase runs in its own fresh sandbox (Table 9 ). No phase sees the benchmark’s tests, reference solutions (its oracle), verifier, or rewards. Every phase runs as the unprivileged agent user, and those files are restricted to root. A verifier is uploaded only after a cold or warm execution has finished, for scoring, so it never guides compilation or triggers recovery. The trace the compiler reads excludes provider reasoning and redacts credentials. Programs run in the agent’s starting directory and read the source skills’ files from a fixed read-only path. Environment variables named like keys, tokens, or passwords are removed from their environment.

summary_override.summary_zh: SkillCache 将已完成调用的工具轨迹编译成参数化 capsule，包含程序和自然语言步骤。宿主在沙箱回放候选，把失败诊断反馈给编译 Agent 修复，通过后供后续请求复用，原技能保留作恢复路径。纳入的是这条执行反馈修订组件的闭环；当前 warm 执行后的持续学习仍属未来工作。回放主要检查原请求条件，不能保证任意新请求正确，节省也需结合编译成本和复用次数判断。
summary_override.summary_en: SkillCache compiles a completed invocation trace into a parameterized capsule of programs and natural-language steps. A host replays candidates in a sandbox, returns failure diagnostics to the compiler agent for repair, and retains qualified capsules for later requests while keeping the source skill for recovery. This execution-feedback repair loop qualifies as component evolution; continued learning from warm executions remains future work. Replay uses the original request conditions, so it does not guarantee arbitrary new requests, and savings depend on compilation cost and reuse frequency.

items.quick_evidence_boundary: Fulltext claims are not relabeled as abstract-only quick evidence.
items.reason_zh: 从完成调用的执行轨迹生成带源码与绑定的 capsule，宿主回放收集真实程序失败并反馈给编译 Agent 修复，合格工件再用于后续请求。纳入的是可执行技能组件的生成/反馈修订/保留；底层 Claude Code Harness 和编译提示固定，不能把 warm 期恢复状态当作持续学习。
items.modified_object: parameterized reusable capsules containing source programs and natural-language steps
items.feedback: cold execution trace plus failed sandbox replay diagnostics returned with the previous capsule for repair
items.retention: qualified capsule cached for later warm executions and tested under controlled changed requests/models

items.summary_en: SkillCache compiles a completed invocation trace into a parameterized capsule of programs and natural-language steps. A host replays candidates in a sandbox, returns failure diagnostics to the compiler agent for repair, and retains qualified capsules for later requests while keeping the source skill for recovery. This execution-feedback repair loop qualifies as component evolution; continued learning from warm executions remains future work. limits: The fixed underlying Harness and compiler prompt are not the evolved artifacts; the capsule is.
Warm-execution self-improvement is future work, not an implemented ongoing loop.
Replay at original values can admit hard-coded values that fail changed-request probes.
Controlled request-change probes use a selected subset of successful cold tasks.
Production retrieval, invalidation and security lifecycle are not evaluated.
All experiments use SkillsBench and Claude Code; no broader-generalization claim.
